findings.claim: Hiverge's CIFAR-10 record (94.02% in 1.98 s) runs Muon with only 3 unrolled Newton-Schulz iterations, using retuned coefficients (a=3.4576, b=-4.7391, c=2.0843). Filters are renormalized only periodically: norm_freq = 2 + int(15*progress), so every 2 steps early and every ~17 late. The target-magnitude schedule runs from 0.5012 to 0.0786. The momentum buffer is fp16, Muon momentum is 0.655 and lr 0.205.
findings.relevance: Gives concrete settings for cutting Muon's per-step cost (3 iterations plus sparse renormalization). E011 suggests per-step overhead is only ~5% of train time, so the expected gain is ≤1–2%.

findings.claim: Other Hiverge hyperparameters: label smoothing 0.09; SGD (Nesterov, momentum 0.825) with wd = 1.04e-6 × batch size; linear LR decay 1 - step/total with no warm-up; whitening-bias training only for the first 20% of an epoch; BatchNorm momentum 0.5566; SiLU instead of GELU; batch 1536; 7.65 epochs. Whitening is computed by SVD on only 960 training images (eps 5e-4). Augmentation adds brightness and contrast jitter (ranges 0.14 and 0.13) on top of flip and 2 px translation.
findings.relevance: Several untested axes: LS ~0.1, very low SGD wd, SiLU, colour jitter (Hiverge says it raised validation accuracy) and BN momentum. The 960-image whitening confirms prepare-side whitening cost can be tiny. Batch 1536 is an intermediate point for H5.1.2.

findings.claim: The Hive credits its brightness/contrast jitter with better validation accuracy and gives no per-change ablation. Its other changes (SiLU, SVD whitening init, compiled step, vectorised optimizer, selective TTA) are reported only as a cumulative 2.59 s → 1.99 s.
findings.relevance: Colour jitter is a cheap augmentation (a few elementwise ops on the GPU) that the tree has not tried. It could be a time-neutral accuracy booster, though on CIFAR-10 it was tuned for a 94% target, not for 100 classes. Selective TTA is banned here.

findings.claim: Rethinking 'Batch' in BatchNorm (Wu & Johnson 2021) finds EMA BN statistics inaccurate early in training, at large batch or high LR, and whenever the weights move fast. EMA lags the current model, so its stats mix in older model states. PreciseBN (recompute stats with the final weights fixed, equal weight per batch) is stable with only N = 10^3–10^4 samples and costs ~0.5% when run once per epoch on ImageNet. At the end of a converged 100-epoch run it gained only 23.70 → 23.54% error (0.16 pp).
findings.relevance: Supports the mechanism and the ≤5k-image budget for H1.3.6 and H2.3.3. A 2.5-batch recompute at batch 2000 is in the stable range. The mismatch here is plausibly larger than in converged ImageNet runs: about 9 epochs, BN momentum ~0.6, and the final weights are a Lookahead average whose BN buffers do not match any single trajectory point. Expect a gain around 0.1–0.3 pp, not ≥0.5.

findings.claim: Turbo-Muon adds AOL preconditioning (column scaling by the inverse sqrt of the Gram row sums, reusing the Gram matmul) and drops one of five NS iterations. On the CIFAR-10 airbench 94% speedrun it saved only 0.8% (1.359 → 1.348 s); on NanoGPT 2.8%. Accuracy was equivalent across 2–5 iterations.
findings.relevance: Independent evidence that NS iteration cuts are worth ≤1% end to end on airbench-scale CNNs. H1.2.3's ≥1.5% threshold is optimistic unless the NS share here is larger than in airbench94 (E006 measured +3.8% for Muon before compile and CUDA graphs).

findings.claim: Practical Efficiency of Muon for Pretraining: Muon keeps data efficiency at batch sizes far beyond the critical batch, better than AdamW. Convergence Bound and Critical Batch Size of Muon: theory and experiments that bound Muon's critical batch size. Both are LLM or small-scale studies; neither covers CIFAR CNNs.
findings.relevance: Weak support for H5/H5.1: raising batch 2000 → 2500 under Muon should cost little accuracy per epoch. With per-step overhead ~5% (E011), the time gain mostly comes from better GPU use at 20/24 px, so ≥1.5% is plausible but not assured.

findings.claim: Drop-Muon (randomized progressive training): each step samples a minimum active layer and updates and backprops only from that layer up, so backprop is truncated below it. An 'epoch-shift' distribution moves the mass from shallow to deep layers over training. On 3-layer CNNs it reached the same accuracy up to 1.4× faster on MNIST and about 1.2× on Fashion-MNIST, with only small gains on CIFAR-10.
findings.relevance: A Muon-native variant of H2.6 (FreezeOut). It supports truncating backward through early layers late in training, but the CIFAR-10 evidence is weak and the models are tiny.

findings.claim: FreezeOut (cubic schedule, t0 ≈ 0.8, LR annealed per layer) gave ~20% wall-clock speedup with no accuracy loss for Wide ResNet on CIFAR-100, up to 20% with ~3% loss for DenseNet, and no benefit for VGG-16. The authors say skip connections appear necessary. These were 100-epoch runs.
findings.relevance: Supports H2.6 for residual nets but in long, near-converged schedules. In a ~9-epoch run the early layers are still learning late, and airbench groups are VGG-like with limited skips, so the accuracy cost may exceed the 0.2 pp bound in H2.6.1. Freezing only whitening plus group 1 for the last 25% saves at most a few percent.

findings.claim: MosaicML's Selective Backprop card reports ~10% time savings: ResNet-56 on CIFAR-10 went 35m33s → 32m36s with 93.16 → 93.32% accuracy. The defaults are start 0.5, end 0.9, keep 0.5, interrupt 2 and scale_factor 0.5. The card warns it 'may harm performance on short training schedules' and helps less when compute is the bottleneck, and it needs ≥33% of examples dropped to pay for the extra forward.
findings.relevance: These are the exact settings in H2.4.2. Even in long runs the gain is ~8–10%, and the card flags short schedules as a risk. With compute already the bottleneck here, the ≥4% saving at ≤0.2 pp loss is a long shot.

findings.claim: When does loss-based prioritization fail? (CIFAR-10, 100 epochs): Selective Backprop gives a 2–3× backprop-count speedup on clean data. It fails or badly degrades when high-loss examples are noisy, mislabeled or ambiguous, because loss cannot separate hard-but-informative examples from noisy ones.
findings.relevance: CIFAR-100 has more ambiguous, fine-grained and near-mislabeled examples than CIFAR-10. Top-loss selection on 100 classes after ~9 epochs will over-sample such examples, another reason to expect H2.4 to underperform.

findings.claim: airbench96_faster (96.00% in 27.3 s, n=200) uses a 32/64/64-wide proxy net, trained in its own preliminary phase, to keep the highest-loss 512 of each 1024 batch for the main model. It runs 45 epochs with LS 0.2, the Lookahead alpha 0.95^5·(t/T)^3 schedule and TTA level 2.
findings.relevance: The only airbench evidence for proxy selection comes from a 45-epoch, 96% regime with a separate proxy training phase. That fixed proxy cost cannot amortize in a ~6 s, ~9-epoch run.

findings.claim: Two-stage label smoothing (TSLA): LS 0.1 early, then dropped for the rest of training. On CIFAR-100 with ResNet-18 (200 epochs, step LR): baseline 76.87%, LS throughout 77.77%, TSLA(160) 77.96%, TSLA(180) 78.04% (std ~0.2). LS mainly speeds early convergence; dropping it late helps the final phase.
findings.relevance: Suggests a new H1.3/H2.3.4-style test: LS 0.3 for most of training, lowered or set to 0 for the final ~10–20% of steps (where the EMA is formed). The literature gain is small (+0.2 pp, within ~1 std). It is near-zero cost but the payoff is unsure, especially since E013 found LS flat between 0.2 and 0.3.

findings.claim: The only public CIFAR-100 speedrun recipe found gets 75.29% in 8.11 s on a Modal A100-SXM4. It is an airbench96 port with SGD lr 9.0, wd 0.012, LS 0.3, 8.5 epochs, widths 128/384/576. Muon lost to SGD at every size in that team's tests and was removed. The PR page itself now returns 404.
findings.relevance: The current tip (6.02 s, held-out 0.7541) already beats the best public CIFAR-100 result by ~25%. That team's negative Muon result conflicts with E006's +0.66 pp, which raises the chance that E006's gain came from batch size or the RNG-stream re-roll (H1.2.2 tests this).

findings.claim: airbench96, without retuning, reaches 79.27% on CIFAR-100 (79.76% with Cutout) versus 77.54% for ResNet-18. In the ablations, alternating flip gives a 27% speedup without TTA but 21% with TTA.
findings.relevance: Confirms that alternating flip is worth more when TTA is off, which supports keeping it (H1.4). The CIFAR-100 numbers come from long runs and say nothing about short-run hyperparameters.

findings.claim: Fable's CIFAR-10 record (1.828 s vs Hiverge 1.978 s, about -7.6% net of specification gaming) used progressive resizing 24 → 28 → 32 in 4 of 5 runs, plus pooling, CUDA-graph and optimizer-fusion work. Other frontier models got ~23% over airbench mainly by trimming the schedule from 10.5 to 9.0–9.75 epochs.
findings.relevance: Matches the tree's finding that resizing plus the epoch dial are the main levers and systems work is second-order. Beyond what E007 already used, the source gives no further evidence on resolution schedules.

findings.claim: ImageNet speedruns (FFCV, fast.ai DAWNBench) schedule batch size and LR per resolution, with larger batches at low resolution to keep the GPU saturated. FFCV goes 160 → 192 px and switches 75% of the way through training.
findings.relevance: Points to a batch-size-per-phase variant the tree has not tried: a larger batch in the 20/24 px phases, where small maps underuse tensor cores (H6.1), and 2000 at 32 px. Combined with Muon's tolerance of large batches, this could recover some of the low-res efficiency loss.

structured_output.summary: The external evidence mostly narrows the open branches rather than opening new big levers. (1) Systems: Muon NS cuts are worth ≤1% end to end on airbench-scale nets (Turbo-Muon 0.8% on the CIFAR-10 speedrun). Hiverge's 3-iteration NS with sparse renormalization gives concrete settings for H1.2.3, but expect ≤1–2%. (2) Data selection: Selective Backprop and proxy filtering helped only in long schedules (~10% savings at 100+ epochs; airbench96_faster runs 45 epochs). MosaicML warns of harm on short schedules, and loss-based selection degrades on ambiguous or noisy examples, a real risk for CIFAR-100. H2.4 looks unlikely. (3) FreezeOut works for residual nets on CIFAR-100 in 100-epoch runs and not for VGG-like nets. Drop-Muon shows only small CIFAR-10 gains, so H2.6.1's ≤0.2 pp bound in a 9-epoch run is doubtful. (4) BN recompute: PreciseBN literature supports 10^3–10^4 samples being enough and EMA statistics lagging under fast-moving weights. The averaged Lookahead weights plus BN momentum ~0.6 make a mismatch plausible, so H1.3.6/H2.3.3 are cheap, worthwhile tests with a likely gain of 0.1–0.3 pp. (5) Untried accuracy boosters from Hiverge: brightness/contrast jitter, LS ~0.09, SiLU, BN momentum ~0.56, very low SGD wd, LR decay with no warm-up. Two-stage label smoothing (drop LS late) gives about +0.2 pp on CIFAR-100. (6) Batch size: LLM studies say Muon keeps data efficiency at large batch, which weakly supports H5.1.1. ImageNet speedruns pair larger batches with low-resolution phases, an untried per-phase batch-schedule variant. (7) The only public CIFAR-100 speedrun recipe (8.11 s, SGD airbench96 port) found Muon worse than SGD, which conflicts with E006 and makes H1.2.2 (is the gain from Muon or from batch size/RNG?) worth settling. The current tip at about 6.0 s already beats every public CIFAR-100 result found.
